newsitem.title: USA: Morgan, Dean Witter plans spawn job fears.
newsitem.headline: Morgan, Dean Witter plans spawn job fears.

text.p: Amid the hoopla surrounding the proposed merger between Morgan Stanley & Co and Dean Witter Reynolds & Co announced on Wednesday, fixed-income employees at the firms expressed concern over the deal.

At a press conference Wednesday morning, senior officials of Morgan Stanley and Dean Witter stressed that there would be a minimum of overlap after the merger because the companies had different focuses.
Still, bond market traders and analysts said they feared for their jobs, as both firms have big fixed-income trading desks.
"There are huge overlaps," said one Dean Witter employee, who spoke under the condition of anonymity. "I am worried about my job and my group."

He said news of the planned merger shocked the entire trading floor, noting that only top-level officials knew about the deal until hours before announcement. Executive vice presidents were notified just before midnight (EST) Tuesday, sources said.
"I found out about it from reading the Wall Street Journal," the employee said.
Traders at Morgan Stanley said they were equally surprised, adding they, too, did not know about the deal until stories appeared in the press.
But Kenneth deRegt, managing director at Morgan Stanley, suggested that fears of layoffs were premature.

"There is no preconceived notion how this is going to play out," deRegt said in an interview with Reuters. "We haven't met the people (at Dean Witter) yet. We are going to sit down with them in the very near future and figure out our strategies and synergies."
"We are not going into this with the idea of laying people off," he added. "Where there is overlap, we may have to make choices."

DeRegt, who heads Morgan's fixed-income department, said it was possible there would be no job cuts. Dean Witter's customer base is individual retail accounts, while Morgan Stanley focuses more on institutional clients, he said.
"This is not like the Chase-Chemical situation," he said, referring to the big bank merger last spring. "There is not a great deal of overlap."
"We will be more effective in fixed income," deRegt said. "We want to be as strong as we possibly can be."

The new company -- to be called Morgan Stanley, Dean Witter, Discover & Co -- would become what officials called the "preeminent" global financial services firm, with a market capitalization of more than $21 billion.
In making the announcement, Richard Fisher, Morgan Stanley's chairman, said the deal was purely a "revenue enhancement opportunity, not a way to reduce costs."

Philip Purcell, Dean Witter's chairman and chief executive, said a merger would combine Morgan Stanley's strengths in investment banking, institutional sales and trading with Dean Witter's force in retail distribution and asset gathering.
He said Morgan would gain a bigger presence in the United States, while Dean Witter -- especially its Discover card unit -- will gain more global exposure.

The move comes less than a month after a restructuring at Morgan Stanley. In January, the firm formed a securities division comprising investment banking, equities, equity research, fixed income, commodities and foreign exchange. Previously, equities and investment banking were seperate units, while fixed income, commodities and forex constituted a third group.
